notes: Statute sets the zero-rate threshold at $2,500 (single) / $5,000 (joint, surviving spouse, head of household) and the tax commission applies the factor each year; 4,811 is the 2025 single figure. The threshold uses the CPI for the calendar year before the tax year, so the 2026 figure uses 2025 CPI.

quote: (j) In the case of an individual, there shall be allowed as a deduction from gross income either paragraph (1) or (2) of this subsection at the option of the taxpayer: (1) The standard deduction as defined in section 63 of the Internal Revenue Code;
section: Idaho Code 63-3022(j)(1), 63-3004 (IRC as in effect January 1, 2026); federal 26 U.S.C. 63(c)(4) and 63(f)
notes: Idaho has no standard deduction table of its own: it takes the federal one by reference, so the amounts move with the federal inflation adjustment. 63-3004: 'the Internal Revenue Code as amended and in effect on the first day of January 2026' (https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title63/T63CH30/SECT63-3004/). Federal text read on Cornell LII (secondary; federal code, not a state matter): '(4) Adjustments for inflation In the case of any taxable year beginning in a calendar year after 1988, each dollar amount contained in paragraph (2)(B), (2)(C), or (5) or subsection (f) shall be increased by an amount equal to ... the cost-of-living adjustment determined under section 1(f)(3)...'. Official uscode.house.gov address could not be fetched. Federal conformity is re-enacted each year, so the figures follow whatever federal figures apply. The 2025 federal amounts (15,750 / 31,500 / 23,625; aged 2,000 / 1,600) match the batch.

quote: For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2004, the personal exemption shall be: (i) the exemption in the previous year plus $275 if the inflation-adjusted growth in baseline taxes in the fiscal year ending the June 30 of the previous year exceeds 2.5 per cent and the inflation-adjusted change in baseline taxes for each consecutive 3 month period reported by the commissioner between August and December of the previous year is greater than 0; or (ii) the personal exemption in effect for the prior year. ... The personal exemption shall not exceed $4,400. ... (C) an additional exemption of seven hundred dollars if the taxpayer had attained the age of sixty-five before the close of his taxable year.
section: M.G.L. c. 62, s. 3(B)(b)(1)(A) (single/separate; 1A head of household; joint parallel with +$425 and +$550 steps and caps), s. 3(B)(b)(1)(C) (age 65)
notes: Personal exemption is NOT indexed to a price index. It could step up by a fixed $275 (single), $425 (head of household) or $550 (joint) a year only when state tax revenue growth passes a trigger, and each is capped by statute ('shall not exceed $4,400' for single; the 6,800 and 8,800 figures are the matching caps). Those amounts are already at their caps, so they are flat. Age-65 $700 is a fixed amount with no adjustment clause. The only occurrences of 'inflation' in s. 3 are in this revenue trigger.

quote: New York's pension and annuity subtraction, 'not in excess of twenty thousand dollars', for an individual who has attained 59 1/2 (the Massachusetts DOR TIR 95-9 quoting N.Y. Tax Law); NY Tax Law 612(c)(3-a): 'but not in excess of twenty thousand dollars'

New York's text (read on the NY Senate site) has a fixed $20,000 and no inflation clause in (c)(3-a); the fetch tool only read the first 100,000 characters of the long section, so I could not rule out an adjustment elsewhere in section 612, but none is known. MA c.62 s.2 text contains no $20,000 figure (checked). TIR address: https://www.mass.gov/technical-information-release/tir-95-9-income-taxation-of-contributory-public-employee-pensions-of-other-states

notes: Official Mississippi Code text is only published by LexisNexis; I read the public-record copy of the code (unicourt cic-code-ms, release 74) plus the pending-bill text of 2022 HB 531 on billstatus.ls.state.ms.us (https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2022/html/HB/0500-0599/HB0531IN.htm), which reproduces 27-7-21 as existing law with the same fixed amounts and proposed adding an annual adjustment (that bill did not pass; no later change seen). DATA CHECK: 27-7-21(d) gives head of family $9,500 (the batch says 8,000; the Department of Revenue form treats it as 8,000 plus 1,500 for the qualifying dependent). Mississippi gives one 1,500 age-65 exemption per taxpayer or spouse; the batch lists 750 for married separate, which is the separate-return splitting rule in 27-7-21(h).

quote: (i) For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2017, until the tax year beginning January 1, 2022, a modification shall be allowed for up to fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000), and for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2023, until the tax year beginning January 1, 2024, a modification shall be allowed for up to twenty thousand dollars ($20,000), and for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, a modification shall be allowed for up to fifty thousand dollars ($50,000), of taxable pension and/or annuity income ... (ii) Adjustment for inflation. The dollar amount contained by reference in subsections (c)(9)(i)(A) and (c)(9)(i)(B) of this section shall be increased annually for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2018 ... (vi) For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, the dollar amount contained by reference in subsection (c)(9)(i)(A) shall be adjusted to equal the dollar amount contained in subsection (c)(8)(i)(A), as adjusted for inflation
notes: The cap is written as a stated dollar amount by year (scheduled: $15,000 for 2017-2021/22, $20,000 for 2023, $50,000 from 2025 on). The inflation clause is worded 'dollar amount contained by reference', and (vi) ties it to the (c)(8) AGI limits, so it indexes the AGI limits (2025: $107,000 single / $133,500 joint per the Division of Taxation guide), not the cap. Evidence: the cap stayed at exactly $15,000 through 2022 although the clause has applied since 2018, and the RI Division of Taxation Retirement Income Guide (PUB 2026-01, https://tax.ri.gov/sites/g/files/xkgbur541/files/2026-02/PUB_2026-01_Retirement_Income_Guide.pdf) says the 2025 change 'does not change the qualifying income thresholds' and states the cap as a flat $50,000 per person. The statute's wording is ambiguous enough that medium confidence is right. Both listed reliefs (ri_pension_annuity_modification and the later-births one) fall under the same (c)(9) text. Section 44-30-12 was read on webserver.rilegislature.gov (http only; https returns 404).
